answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1903–1941 · New York Yankees first baseman · Baseball Hall of Fame, 1939
answer.sourceLine: This is the last sentence of Gehrig’s farewell address at Yankee Stadium on 4 July 1939, and the wording here is the one his estate’s own site ↗ publishes. We file it as attributed rather than verified for one honest reason: only four sentences of the speech survive on film, and the contemporary newspaper reports we could read quote the opening lines and stop. Even Sports Illustrated, reprinting the estate’s text, renders this sentence with different words.
answer.confidenceText: Genuine beyond serious doubt, but the wording is not pinned to a contemporary source.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 4 July 1939 — the closing line of the farewell address, Yankee Stadium
lougehrig.com, the estate’s official site, and Wikiquote

source.excerpt: When you have a wife who has been a tower of strength and shown more courage than you dreamed existed — that’s the finest I know. So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I’ve got an awful lot to live for.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced Lou Gehrig page ↗ carries this sentence in exactly this wording and attributes it to the “Speech made on Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day at Yankee Stadium (July 4, 1939)”. It gives no citation beyond the occasion.
The estate’s own site, lougehrig.com ↗, publishes the full address ending on the same sentence. Most modern reprints trace back to this text.
The wording is not stable. Sports Illustrated ↗ reprints the address citing lougehrig.com and still ends it differently: “I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for.”

We looked for a contemporary printing and did not find one. The three 5 July 1939 pages we read — the Evening Star ↗, the Washington Daily News ↗ and the Waterbury Democrat ↗ — all quote the opening “luckiest man” passage and none of them reaches the close, and a search of the Library of Congress’s digitised 1939 newspapers for the phrase returns nothing. That is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence — but it is why this page says attributed.

It is also why the sentence is unfamiliar. Steve Wulf notes ↗ that only four sentences of newsreel survive, and that when Major League Baseball marked the speech’s 75th anniversary it saved “the last, best lines — words that Cooper never spoke” for the end: the 1942 film cuts them.
source.excerptNote: That is the closing of the text lougehrig.com publishes as the Farewell Address ↗. Sports Illustrated’s “Full Text of Lou Gehrig’s Farewell Speech” ↗ reprints the same address, cites lougehrig.com as its source, and ends it “So I close in saying that I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for.” Two texts, one lineage, two sentences.
source.rightsNote: The address was delivered in 1939, long after 1930, so we assert no public-domain status for it. The text reproduced here is the one published by the Gehrig estate’s official site. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Lou Gehrig
author.heading: About Lou Gehrig
author.metaLine: 1903–1941 · New York Yankees first baseman · Baseball Hall of Fame, 1939
author.bio: Henry Louis “Lou” Gehrig (19 June 1903 – 2 June 1941) played seventeen seasons at first base for the New York Yankees and was nicknamed “the Iron Horse” for a streak of 2,130 consecutive games that stood for fifty-six years. He took himself out of the lineup on 2 May 1939; the Mayo Clinic’s diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis was made public on his thirty-sixth birthday, 19 June, and the Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day two weeks later. He died less than two years afterwards, and in the United States the disease still carries his name.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody credits this sentence to anyone but Gehrig. The trouble is that it comes in at least two forms, and the version most people have heard is a film that cuts it entirely.

items.why: SI’s full text ↗ ends “I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for” — while citing lougehrig.com ↗, which ends “I might have been given a bad break, but I’ve got an awful lot to live for.” One of the two has been smoothed, and there is no recording to say which.
Gary Cooper’s speech ends on “the luckiest man on the face of the earth” instead. Wulf ↗ calls these closing lines “words that Cooper never spoke”. If the sentence sounds unfamiliar, that is why.
Pages that present this sentence as a documented quotation rarely say where it was first printed. We could not find it in a contemporary newspaper, and we are not going to imply that we did.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Gehrig’s closing line, published in this wording by his estate ↗ and Wikiquote ↗ — but the exact words rest on a text no 1939 source we could reach confirms.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The speech is remembered for its opening. Its ending is the harder sentence: a man of thirty-six whose diagnosis had been made public a fortnight earlier, standing in front of sixty-one thousand people, declining to be their tragedy. He was dead within two years.
The wording gets tidied in reuse — “a bad break” smoothed to “a tough break”, “I’ve got” to “I have”. Small edits, and they are the reason this page is filed as attributed.
detailsBody: The sentence before it is the one Gehrig reportedly cared most about: “When you have a wife who has been a tower of strength and shown more courage than you dreamed existed — that’s the finest I know.” Eleanor Gehrig later fought the makers of The Pride of the Yankees over their rewriting of the address, telling Samuel Goldwyn that departing from the original would “lose all of the simple charm.”

For what it is worth, the parts of the speech that are documented in 1939 print survive in more than one wording too. The Associated Press and United Press transcriptions of the opening sentence, filed the same afternoon from the same microphone, do not match each other — so an unstable closing line is the expected condition of this text, not a sign that something is wrong with it.
context.pull: Sixty-one thousand people, twenty-three months to live, and he closed by declining to be a tragedy.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 5 July 1939, page 14, in an Associated Press report by Sid Feder, prints: 'Several times his voice broke and a sob escaped as he announced, "Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth."'

The Washington Daily News, 5 July 1939, page 28, prints a different transcription: 'For the past two weeks,' he said, 'you've been reading about what a bad break I had. But I want to say now that I'm the luckiest man on the face of the earth.'

The Waterbury Democrat (Waterbury, Conn.), 5 July 1939, page 16, in a United Press report by Leslie Avery headlined 'LOU GEHRIG CRIES AS 62,000 FANS STAND TO CHEER', prints the same United Press wording as the Washington Daily News.

Steve Wulf, ESPN, 4 July 2014: 'only a small snippet of the newsreel footage, only four sentences, has survived'; the 'luckiest man' line 'came at the very beginning of Gehrig's speech, but for dramatic effect, it's at the end of Cooper's' in the 1942 film The Pride of the Yankees; the real address runs 277 words to the film's 169.

Wikiquote's Lou Gehrig page sources both 'Fans, for the past two weeks you have been reading about a bad break I got. Yet today, I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth' and 'So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for' to the speech made on Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day at Yankee Stadium, July 4, 1939.

The official lougehrig.com 'Farewell Address' page gives the closing sentence as 'So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for.' and the opening as '...the luckiest man on the face of this earth.'

Sports Illustrated's 'Full Text of Lou Gehrig's Farewell Speech', which cites lougehrig.com as its source, gives the closing sentence differently: 'So I close in saying that I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for.'

Wikipedia's Lou Gehrig article gives the speech text with explicit footnotes recording variant readings: 'Also reported as: "...you have been reading about the bad break I got"', 'Also reported as: "Yet today"', and 'Also reported as: "this"' for 'the face of the Earth'. It gives his dates as June 19, 1903 - June 2, 1941.
